newsitem.title: UK: Danube dam lets toxic algae thrive, report says.
newsitem.headline: Danube dam lets toxic algae thrive, report says.

text.p: Damming the Danube has let poisonous algae take over from the previous benign residents of the Black Sea, researchers reported on Wednesday.

The Danube was dammed in 1972 at the "Iron Gates" where it forms the border between Yugoslavia and Romania. The Danube provides about 70 percent of the freshwater input into the Black Sea and thus is important to its ecology.
Since then, silicates in the river have decreased by about two-thirds, Venugopalan Ittekkot of the University of Hamburg and colleagues wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
They said this had affected the balance among the tiny organisms that form the base of the food chain. Silicon-based diatoms had given way to toxic algae blooms.

"Our results strongly suggest the damming of the Danube has been instrumental in causing the observed changes in Black Sea surface waters, and that the large number of dams in operation around the world today could similarly affect the food web structure and biogeochemical cycling in coastal seas," they wrote.
John Milliman, a marine scientist at Virginia's College of William and Mary, said the report illustrated how damaging dams can be if they are not designed properly.

"What makes (this) paper particularly important is the possible clues it may offer to environmental problems that could occur not only in estuaries and coastal areas adjacent to dammed rivers, but also in larger bodies of water such as the Black Sea," Milliman wrote in a commentary.
Milliman said Egypt's Aswan Dam clearly helped fight drought but noted it meant less sediment reached the Mediterranean, with effects ranging from a lower fish catch to dying coastal lagoons.
In the Mississippi River delta, lack of sediment was causing a loss of coastal land, he added.
